items.headline: Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight MoE
items.diff_narrative: The open-weight-model lead slot repeats but inverts on nearly every axis. Yesterday Inkling was a US neolab's 975B-total / 41B-active MoE that openly conceded it was not the strongest model available and sold customizability, routing straight into the Tinker fine-tuning platform. Today's lead is Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter sparse MoE — close to triple the total scale — that instead claims frontier-adjacency outright, taking first on the Frontend Code Arena at 1,679 ahead of Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol and landing fourth of 189 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. The distribution shape also flips: Inkling shipped open weights on day 0 with Together serving and Unsloth same-day support, whereas Kimi K3 is an API-first debut at roughly $3/$15 per million tokens with the full weights promised July 27 — an open-weights follow-through rather than a same-day drop. And where Inkling read as a second US neolab entering the open race, Kimi K3 returns the story to Chinese labs reaching frontier-adjacent results while working around US compute-export limits, a thread that recurs in today's WAIC hardware item.

items.headline: Fireworks AI raises a $1.5B Series D at a $17.5B valuation
items.diff_narrative: The business slot moves up the stack and from a public filing to a private round. Yesterday's number was TSMC's audited Q2 — US$40.20 billion in revenue quantifying AI demand at the wafer, where the binding constraint is leading-edge supply. Today's number is a venture round one layer up: Fireworks AI's $1.5 billion Series D at a $17.5 billion valuation, past $1 billion in ARR and 40 trillion tokens a day, more than 95% of them served from models specialized on customers' own data rather than general-purpose frontier endpoints. The two mark the same demand curve at opposite ends of the stack — TSMC rationing the silicon everyone queues for, Fireworks monetizing the managed-inference tier that turns general models into specialized ones — with NVIDIA present on both, as the accelerator supplier downstream of TSMC and now a strategic investor in the serving layer. Fireworks also operationalizes yesterday's Inkling thesis: the bet that enterprises would rather own specialized models than rent frontier endpoints is precisely the shift its business is built on.

items.headline: Claude Code ships v2.1.212 with default-on agent-safety limits
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday the agent-safety story was a fine-tuning framework borrowing the vocabulary; today it is the coding agent shipping it default-on. Unsloth's v0.1.49-beta had added a four-level tool-call permission selector with workspace isolation — a tuning tool converging on the permission-gating grammar coding agents wrote first. Claude Code v2.1.212 is that grammar hardening inside the agent itself: session-wide caps on WebSearch calls and subagent spawns, defaulting to 200 each, to stop runaway search-and-delegation loops, plus fail-closed permission fixes where Bash checks now reject file-descriptor redirect forms the analyzer parses differently, a Windows PowerShell 5.1 permission bypass is closed, and any command over 10,000 characters always prompts. The through-line is that runaway-loop budgets and fail-closed gating are no longer an aftermarket add-on but a default in a mainstream agent — and today's Check Point report names exactly the threat this answers: malicious instructions planted in the configuration files an agent auto-loads every session.

items.headline: WAIC 2026 opens in Shanghai with a domestic-silicon push led by Dongfang Suanxin's DF1000
items.diff_narrative: The silicon story flips from the leading edge to the workaround. Yesterday TSMC's Q2 was the leading-edge-supply narrative — 2nm ramping, advanced nodes at 77% of wafer revenue, demand rationed by wafer supply, everyone downstream queuing for the same process shrink. Today WAIC 2026 opens in Shanghai with the inverse strategy on the floor: among its 108 exhibited chips the sharpest signal is Dongfang Suanxin's DF1000, a mature 14nm accelerator with no HBM that leans on software-defined design and 3D-stacked near-memory computing to claim 6.4 TB/s of bandwidth — roughly a third above an H200 — even as raw compute lands near half. Where TSMC wins by shrinking the node, Dongfang and the ten-plus domestic compute-chip vendors beside it are trying to route around leading-edge lithography and HBM entirely, through architecture and advanced packaging, explicitly designing around US export limits — the same compute-export-workaround thread that today's Kimi K3 carries at the model layer.

items.headline: Check Point's AI Security Report 2026 finds AI now runs live intrusions autonomously
items.diff_narrative: The security slot turns from the defender's ledger to the attacker's. Yesterday's item was patch volume — Microsoft's record 570-CVE Patch Tuesday, with an AI-surface cluster of Copilot flaws and AI-powered discovery cited as the reason the count keeps climbing, still fundamentally a story of bugs being found and shipped as fixes faster. Check Point's AI Security Report 2026 is the offensive mirror: it argues AI has crossed from development aid to live attack operator, documenting intrusions where AI ran exploitation workflows autonomously — thousands of commands across dozens of sessions — and one operator producing an 88,000-line command-and-control framework in under a week. Its structural finding lands on the agent-security thread running through today's slate: a durable bypass that plants malicious instructions in the configuration files an agent auto-loads every session — precisely the poisoning vector today's Claude Code guardrails and yesterday's Unsloth permission gating are built against — now measured at scale, with longer malicious payloads up roughly fivefold from March to May, rather than shown as a lab demo, and set alongside the year's Cursor and MCP incidents.

items.headline: AI events to plan around now: the AGI Summit hits San Francisco this weekend
items.diff_narrative: The roster carries forward intact and, unusually, adds nothing new — yesterday's two fresh entries, OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason and PyTorch Conference North America, are now folded into the standing calendar, and today brings no additions. What moves is the clock: the AGI Summit at the Palace of Fine Arts is no longer 'this weekend' but tomorrow, July 18-19, with Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta and Tesla among 200-plus speakers; AMD's Advancing AI follows July 22-23 with the Instinct MI450 and Zen 6 EPYC Venice expected; and the July 31 Hot Chips early rate still gates the early-August Las Vegas security block of Black Hat, DEF CON's AI Village and the AI Risk Summit. The autumn stack — the September 29 DevDay and Pier 48 collision, PyTorch on October 20-21, GitHub Universe, re:Invent, NeurIPS and IEEE-RAS Humanoids — is unchanged; the one decision that has actually moved to the front is the AGI Summit, which now has to be settled today.
